doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

title: First hearing bebop, Dixieland and then real New Orleans jazz
summary: White first heard bebop and Dixieland, but traditional New Orleans clarinet seemed to express who he was; he sought out records and older players at Jazz Fest.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah I’ll have to check it out. But yeah, you know it’s a funny thing. I listened to a lot of different music before I got to the authentic New Orleans jazz style and sound. The first jazz I actually heard was bebop because there was a little of that on the radio and they used to have live broadcasts from this place called Lou and Charlie’s and they featured you know some of the great modern jazz musicians in New Orleans like Ellis Marsalis and, you know, people like that. And I used to listen to those things. And then there was some jazz shows that had modern jazz, and I heard that. And then I also heard Dixieland like. But none of that really – I liked the modern jazz –
Did you hear Buddy DeFranco at the time?

No. It was much later when I heard Buddy DeFranco. I didn’t even know clarinets played, you know, bebop style ‘til later. And then I heard that music, I liked it as a listener, but it didn’t speak to my – so when I heard the real New Orleans jazz it seemed to define what my life was about, what it felt like to be in and from New Orleans. It felt like that music was the way we think, the way we talk, the way older people thought. It was an expression of life. And so it immediately grabbed me, like this is what it means to be from New Orleans. This is our language so to speak. And it just – it wasn’t a choice, it was something that just grabbed me. And so I started listening to that. And I heard Dixieland clarinet players a lot, because that was more promoted and better known and I

heard that, whether it be from people who played on Bourbon Street or on Lawrence Welk or something. But when I heard the real New Orleans jazz clarinet original style, it just spoke to me. So I started to listen to a lot of that kind of stuff, wherever I could find it. But it was hard to find back in the day, no YouTube and recordings were rare. So I sought out recordings. But it was a long process. And I started going to the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival and I got to hear some older players there. So it was a combination of hearing recordings and older players playing live. I heard Willie Humphrey, Louis Catrell, Raymond Burke, Joseph Thomas, and then I heard Barney Bigard.
